analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacists automatically substitute cheaper biosimilar insulin for brand-name insulin.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on September 8, 2020 and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the term ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current FDA rules, a copy of a biologic drug like insulin ('biosimilar') only becomes 'interchangeable' — meaning a pharmacist can swap it for the brand-name version without going back to the prescribing doctor — after meeting extra requirements. This bill would declare any FDA-approved biosimilar insulin automatically interchangeable. That would make it far easier for patients to get a cheaper version of insulin at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of Americans who use insulin, including people with Type 1 diabetes who face some of the highest drug prices in the country. Automatic substitution means a cheaper biosimilar could fill the prescription without a new visit or a new prescription, and pharmacies would have clearer authority to stock and dispense the cheaper product. Biosimilar manufacturers would also benefit from a bigger, faster route to market.

how_it_helps.text: Declares any insulin the FDA finds biosimilar to a reference product to be interchangeable, so it can be substituted at the pharmacy without the prescriber's involvement.
Removes the extra review step and delay current law imposes before a biosimilar insulin can be treated as interchangeable, applying to products already approved and products approved later.
Shortens the exclusivity period for the first interchangeable biosimilar insulin in certain patent-dispute scenarios, letting a second competitor reach patients sooner.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name insulin makers — Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi — whose patented products would face direct substitution at the pharmacy, eroding sales. Pharmacy benefit managers, which negotiate rebates on brand insulin, would also lose some control over which product patients receive.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the FDA's case-by-case determination that a biosimilar can be safely and effectively swapped for the specific brand a doctor prescribed; under current law, interchangeability requires meeting additional requirements beyond biosimilarity.
The bill does not cap insulin prices directly — it relies on market competition, so savings depend on how many biosimilar products actually reach the market and how they are priced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: insulin list prices have been among the most notorious in American medicine, and lowering the barrier to substitution is a practical way to get patients the cheaper product without new paperwork. The cost is a trade-off in regulatory caution — FDA's interchangeability standard exists to confirm a swap is safe for the individual product, and this bill waives it for insulin across the board. On balance it is a well-aimed, if narrow, competition bill; its main weakness is that it does not itself guarantee lower prices, only easier access to whatever cheaper products come to market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in September 2020, and the committee took no action on it before the two-year term ran out.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman introduced the Biosimilar Insulin Access Act of 2020 on September 8, 2020.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over drug regulation.
No markup, vote, or further committee action followed; the only subsequent activity was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on September 16, 2020.
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill; no version passed either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name insulin makers kept a market in which biosimilar copies could not be substituted at the pharmacy without the extra FDA interchangeability process. Patients who pay insulin prices gained nothing; the bill died with no hearing and no vote.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 8, 2020 and delivered introductory remarks on September 16.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 8, 2020 and took no further action — no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican sponsored and one Democrat cosponsored, a small bipartisan pair, but no opposition was ever recorded because the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.industry: Brand-name insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: These companies dominate the US insulin market. Making every FDA-approved biosimilar insulin interchangeable would let pharmacists substitute cheaper copies directly, cutting into brand-name sales.

The bill gives biosimilar insulin a faster, cheaper route to patients by waiving the extra interchangeability review and shortening exclusivity in certain cases, and their gain to patients is the same thing: lower prices.

Insulin is a major rebate business for PBMs, which negotiate on brand-name products; automatic pharmacy substitution of cheaper biosimilars would weaken their control over which product a patient gets.
